title: Why AI Agents Will Need Their Own Bank Accounts — Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
body:
Lincoln Murr, head of AI product at Coinbase, explains agentic finance: agents that pay with money and agents that grow it. He covers the path from AgentKit, an early experiment giving an AI a wallet, to x402, an open standard built on the long-unused HTTP 402 "payment required" code. x402 now handles hundreds of millions of agent transactions a month. Other topics are microtransactions as a replacement for the ad economy, agents running trades on simple instructions, and what two years of building taught Coinbase. Trust is earned step by step, and the AI is the enabler, not the product. He ends with a look at agents that can pay for their own upkeep.

title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
body:
The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries.
Many of these companies are also members of the [NVIDIA Inception](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/) program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal.
NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through [NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/training/) open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources.
An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch.
Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day:
Qatium’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the [NVIDIA cuGraph](https://github.com/rapidsai/cugraph) library, the [NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo](https://developer.nvidia.com/physicsnemo) framework and [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day.
OneCareAI, a research spin-off from BSC, used [NVIDIA NIM](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/products/nim-microservices/) microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs.
Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the [NVIDIA Nemotron 3](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open model family and the open source [NVIDIA NeMo Curator](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Curator) library.
Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI, Elna Health, Lokutor, Montevive AI, Oppy, Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging.
The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more.
Learn more about [NVIDIA Inception](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/) and the [BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme](https://bsc-aifactory.eu/accelerator/).

title: My obituary for programming
body:
19th October 2026 - Link Blog
[My obituary for programming](https://dumbmatter.com/2026/10/programming-obituary/) ([via](https://lobste.rs/s/wtobpt/my_obituary_for_programming)) Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code:
Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible.
If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving.
If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real.

title: It's still OK to enjoy programming - Blogomatano
body:
It's still OK to enjoy programming
Published: 2026-10-17
Reading [Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/news) makes me feel like I need to write this: it's still OK to enjoy programming.
Yes, at work, where you are paid to produce value for a business, the economics of purely hand-written code have changed. But that's work. Work is not life. The loudest voices on the internet are the saddest and most infectious.
To throw a tiny counter example in the sea of despair: I still program on the weekends because it is fun. I'm currently learning game programming! My current level of sophistication is a buggy Breakout clone with terrible collision detection. I write it by hand because I enjoy it. I struggle with problems because solving them makes me happy. It doesn't bother me that Claude could one-shot it, because that's not the point.
I also get side-tracked from working on this "game" to study random programming topics. Last weekend was exploring how far I could push type safety in Java using ideas from dependently typed languages like [Agda](https://agda.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html). There is no point to this. It gets tucked away under "interesting ways of thinking about a particular problem." Maybe it will come up in work life. Maybe not. I did it because exploring is was fun[0].
A few weekends ago: [recursion schemes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Recursion_schemes). Technically, this was not fun. I spent hours of banging my head against a wall. In the end, I still don't even know what's valuable about the ideas[1]. But I do know that many of the most beautiful ideas in programming only become clear to me after years of baking in my mind. It's why [entire papers get written about Monoids](http://ozark.hendrix.edu/~yorgey/pub/monoid-pearl.pdf). Maybe one day I'll find a problem that this applies to. Maybe not. I did it because understanding hard things is rewarding.
I write this because I increasingly feel a strange social pressure. It's like I'm not "supposed" to enjoy this any more. As though there's no point or joy to be had in continuing to grow as a human. The more of this doom stream you consume, the more it starts to infect you. Maybe "there is no point," you find yourself thinking. But this disappears as soon as you disconnect.
It's OK to enjoy things[2]. Doing so requires no economic justification.
Footnotes:
[ Fin](https://idris-lang.org/Idris2/base/docs/Data.Fin.html) one day. It is beautiful.

title: Germany Wants to Lead the World in Industrial AI: How NVIDIA Will Help
body:
In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI.
Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing.
The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies.
Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA.
The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI.
Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.”
Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry
Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition.
“We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.”
Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience.
“The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”
Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it.
“That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.”
Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included.
“If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.”
Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution.
“This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.”
Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI.
“I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.”
NVIDIA’s Investments in Germany
Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe.
NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs.
Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace.
Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare.
Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care.
Mirelo, a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen.
Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years.
Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation
Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens [showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory](https://blogs.nvidia.com/gtc-berlin-2026-news/#entry-postlet-siemens-and-nvidia-put-industrial-ai-to-work-in-erlangen), advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%.
NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a [record-breaking simulation](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-runs-record-simulation-of-fault-tolerant-quantum-computing-at-julich-supercomputing-centre) of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date.

title: NVIDIA Advances Agentic Security for Media, From European Public Service Broadcasting to Global Content Production
body:
At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe, Bertelsmann, NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display.
Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration partners, while Adobe Frame.io is accelerating video agent search capabilities with NVIDIA GPUs, helping German TV and film producer UFA find the right moments faster.
Read more about both announcements below.
Sovereign Clouds and Open Models Built for European Broadcasters
The EBU and NVIDIA are expanding the sovereign standards they [introduced](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/european-broadcasting-union-sovereign-ai/) last year for European public service media. The initiative now brings in sovereign cloud providers, open model developers and systems integrators to define how broadcasters can deploy agents while keeping control of their data, infrastructure, models and security.
The EBU is the world’s leading alliance of public service media, with over 115 member organizations in more than 55 countries reaching over 1 billion people. As agents move into newsrooms, production and audience services, those broadcasters need a foundation that protects editorial independence, data sovereignty and national resilience.
The expanded initiative is turning those principles into deployable services. It’ll define requirements and reference architectures for where workloads run, how data is governed, which models power services and how systems stay secure throughout their lifecycle.
“These standards give EBU members a shared foundation to strengthen resilience, retain control and deliver accountable advanced services that sustain audience trust,” said Annsofi Eriksson, chief technology officer at the EBU.
Cloud providers will map the standards to sovereign deployment options:
- Microsoft will bring expertise from Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, including Azure Local and Foundry Local, so broadcasters can process sensitive editorial material locally and keep critical services running when external connectivity is down.
- Nebius offers a platform for broadcasters to train, fine-tune and run their own models on European infrastructure.
Open models give broadcasters the visibility to inspect, evaluate and adapt AI for local languages, archives and editorial policies. [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open models provide a foundation broadcasters can customize for domain-specific applications and public-service requirements.
“Sovereign cloud infrastructure and open models can help Europe’s public service media innovate while protecting data, editorial independence and cultural diversity,” said Delphine Ernotte, CEO of France Télévisions and president of the EBU.
Media-specific consulting and systems integration provided from Qvest and other system integrators to ensure that reference architectures are practical, interoperable and deployable in real world broadcast environments.
Adobe Frame.io Speeds Video Search With NVIDIA Accelerated Computing
Also at the event, Adobe is highlighting its latest enhancements that help creatives search through video data faster.
Adobe is using NVIDIA accelerated computing to help creative teams find and work with video content faster. Its GPU-accelerated search pipeline uses [NVIDIA NVDEC ](https://developer.nvidia.com/video-codec-sdk)for video decoding, [TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt) for optimized AI inference and the [CUDA platform](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-zone) for preprocessing and embedding generation.
Adobe is also advancing GPU-accelerated media ingest using NVIDIA NVENC and NVDEC to accelerate video encoding and decoding, helping production teams process growing media libraries more efficiently.
The results: about 5x faster embedding generation, up to 4x higher throughput and up to 5x lower latency for search processing. A new two-frame-per-second proxy, about 80% smaller than the 360p version it replaces, cuts storage and transfer while keeping the visual detail search needs.
That speed matters for UFA, one of Germany’s leading film and TV producers. It delivers more than 3,500 hours of programming a year, including the daily drama “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten.” When editors build a recap or flashback, they may need a specific reaction or unresolved exchange from as far back as 15 years — something file names and folders can’t surface.
Frame.io semantic search finds moments inside videos by concept, action or setting, and hybrid search adds notes, transcripts and approval status. An editor can search for “a character looking concerned,” narrow by character name and filter to approved footage, then move straight into review.
The work is part of a broader Adobe and NVIDIA collaboration that also spans Adobe Substance 3D, Firefly Foundry and 3D digital twin workflows for enterprises.
Learn more about [NVIDIA technologies for media and entertainment](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/industries/media-and-entertainment/live-media/).

title: Pi Durable: AI agents that survive crashes
body:
Your agent sent 4 of 5 emails… then crashed. A regular coding agent leaves you with a half-finished tool call and a "continue" prayer. Pi Durable checkpoints every task and tool call (SQLite / JSONL), so when the process restarts, the agent resumes where it left off.

It's not a CLI. It's a TypeScript library for building always-on agents, even fully local with Qwen3.5-0.8B on llama.cpp.

Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL [supports⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/cobol) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in [weather forecasting⁠(opens in a new window)](https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/71120) and [nuclear reactor safety analysis⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.nrc.gov/education-regulatory-research/research/computer-codes). Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on.

This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the company, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on.

To measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building new software and preserving what existing software does.

Our latest models show substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.

On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested. GPT‑6 Luna also outperforms GPT‑5.6 Sol, reaching 40.3% at approximately 78% lower estimated API cost.

On our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, nearly saturating the evaluation.

Together, these results show that our models are becoming significantly better at working with a wide range of programming languages, while also becoming more cost-efficient.

## 1. Building SQLite from scratch (MultiLangBench)

MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.

To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database. We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.

We adapted tests from SQLite’s existing test suite to this format. The evaluation measures how much working functionality a model can build over an extended coding session, reporting both test pass rate and API cost.

At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%). Astra scores above 83% in 19 of the 20 languages, with COBOL remaining the hardest at 72%.

GPT‑6 Luna offers a lower-cost option that also improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol in every language tested. At maximum reasoning effort, it reaches an average test pass rate of 40.3%. Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%). These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.

CC#C++COBOLCommon LispFortranGoJavaJavaScriptLeanOCamlPHPPowerShellPythonRubyRustScalaSwiftVisual BasicZig

We are releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite on [GitHub⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/MultiLangBench), along with results for each language. Developers can inspect what the evaluation tests, review performance in the languages they use, and identify gaps that matter for their own work.

## 2. Migrating a COBOL codebase

Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

Successful migration requires understanding both the program’s business logic and COBOL’s specific language behavior. COBOL programs often process financial transactions and business records, where details such as rounding rules and missing-record handling reflect business requirements. For example, COBOL’s fixed-point arithmetic discards excess decimal digits unless rounding is explicitly requested. A rewrite that rounds those values instead can run without errors while producing different financial results.

To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass. Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.

On this evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT‑5.6 Sol’s 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation. These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on.

## Advancing capabilities for enterprise software

These evaluations, alongside direct feedback from developers and enterprise customers, help us see where our models are improving and where they still fall short.

Our goal is to help models apply software engineering skills across more languages: understanding unfamiliar repositories, planning changes, using build tools, running tests, and debugging failures.

You can try our latest models through the API on coding tasks in the languages your team uses. Your feedback on what works, where the models struggle, and which languages or workflows we should focus on next helps shape how we train and evaluate models to better support the software you depend on.

title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
body:
Get the developer newsletter
Product updates, how-tos, community spotlights, and more. Delivered monthly to your inbox.
Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion.
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.
In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.
Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.
Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.
As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.
Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?
With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s [Piper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piper_(source_control_system)) and Meta’s [Sapling](https://sapling-scm.com/),[2](#footnote-2) so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:
Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.
Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.
A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.
Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.
Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.
The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.
It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.
In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,[1](#footnote-1) along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.
This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.
A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.
This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.
A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.
Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.
Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.
In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a da

title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
body:
[
](#torchneuron-running-hf-models-on-aws-trainium-is-easier-than-ever)
TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/hf-torchneuron.md)
[
](#torchneuron)
TorchNeuron
[TorchNeuron](https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/frameworks/torch/index.html) is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile
and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
Read the Pytorch [blog](https://pytorch.org/blog/introducing-torchneuron-native-pytorch-backend-for-aws-trainium/) to learn more about TorchNeuron.
Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx
.
[
](#new-backend-native-interface-in-hf-libraries)
New backend, native interface in HF libraries
To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through [optimum-neuron](https://github.com/huggingface/optimum-neuron). This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.
TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron
as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile
.
For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.
[
](#transformers)
Transformers
[
](#inference)
Inference
Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron
argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.
The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401
from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig
MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B"
MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024
PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron")
world_size = dist.get_world_size()
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
MODEL_ID,
dtype=torch.bfloat16,
distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size),
device_mesh=DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(world_size))),
).eval()
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
[{"role": "user", "content": "The future of AI is"}],
add_generation_prompt=True,
padding=True,
tokenizer_kwargs={"pad_to_multiple_of": PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE},
return_tensors="pt",
)
generation_config = GenerationConfig(
max_new_tokens=128,
do_sample=False,
use_cache=True,
pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
cache_implementation="static",
max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE,
compile_config=CompileConfig(backend="neuron", fullgraph=False, dynamic=False),
)
with torch.no_grad():
output_ids = model.generate(
inputs["input_ids"],
attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],
generation_config=generation_config,
)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0, prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True))
[
](#training)
Training
Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.
Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer
. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.
import os
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser
def main(script_args, training_args, model_args):
# The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660)
torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False
training_args.model_init_kwargs = {
"revision": model_args.model_revision,
"trust_remote_code": training_args.trust_remote_code,
"attn_implementation": model_args.attn_implementation,
"dtype": model_args.dtype,
"device_map": None,
}
if int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1")) > 1:
# The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded
training_args.model_init_kwargs["distributed_config"] = DistributedConfig(
tp_size=int(os.environ.get("TP_SIZE", "1")),
fsdp_size=int(os.environ.get("FSDP_SIZE", "1")),
)
# Prepare dataset
train_dataset = load_dataset(
script_args.dataset_name,
name=script_args.dataset_config,
split=script_args.dataset_train_split,
)
# UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset.
train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns(["messages"])
# Training
trainer = SFTTrainer(
model=model_args.model_name_or_path,
args=training_args,
train_dataset=train_dataset,
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir)
trainer.end()
if __name__ == "__main__":
parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
main(script_args, training_args, model_args)
Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig
with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs
, SFTTrainer
passes it to from_pretrained
, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp
flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.
Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:
- Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in
torch.compile
and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes. torch.compile
on. Passing--torch_compile true
is all it takes: on a Trainium instance,torch.compile
detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.- Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with
HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1
.
The command below launches training with torchrun
, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE
and FSDP_SIZE
set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node
. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.
TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
--model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
--dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
--dataset_train_split train_sft \
--output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
--dtype bfloat16 \
--max_length 2048 \
--packing true \
--packing_strategy wrapped \
--learning_rate 2e-5 \
--warmup_steps 0.03 \
--num_train_epochs 1 \
--logging_steps 2 \
--per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
--gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
--save_only_model true \
--torch_compile true
We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge
instance.
Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model
writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.
[
](#diffusers)
Diffusers
[
](#inference-1)
Inference
Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:
import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP
from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig
# Distributed devices initialization
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron") # TP
dev = torch.neuron.current_device()
mesh = DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(8))) # TP=8
# Pipeline initialization
model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1"
transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained(
model,
subfolder="transformer",
torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP
)
pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained(
model,
transformer=transformer,
torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe.vae.to(dev)
pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)
# Image generation
emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt="A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting", device="cpu") # text encoder stays on CPU
image = pipe(
prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev),
prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None,
height=1024,
width=1024,
num_inference_steps=40,
generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(0), # same noise on every rank
).images[0]
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
image.save("out.png")
You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py
.
More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following [this guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/main/en/training/distributed_inference#writing-a-tensor-parallelism-plan).
[
](#kernels)
Kernels
Make sure to check out the [kernels from the Neuron team](https://huggingface.co/aws-neuron/kernels) as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models.
Neuron kernels can be written using the [Neuron Kernel Interface](https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/nki/index.html) (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.
You can use for example [this kernel](https://huggingface.co/kernels/aws-neuron/vit-encoder-neuron-kernels) to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

](#acknowledgments)
Acknowledgments

title: Together Post-Training: frontier-grade model shaping, the way that fits you
body:
We are introducing Together Post-Training, a new service for building custom models on our platform — both from environment rewards via RL and supervision data via SFT. This service is designed to give you flexible and efficient model shaping without the heavy infra burden.
Together Post-Training makes it easy to define the training loop, while we co-optimize the systems and infrastructure underneath for model quality and training speed. Nothing now stands between you and the best model that is uniquely yours.
The value of custom models
In 2026, training custom models for your AI workloads is no longer a niche topic. Companies are actively exploring it to reduce costs and improve task-specific performance. Instead of fixing model behaviors and improving their efficiency via context or harness engineering, many AI-native and AI-forward organizations are training specialist agents, matching the quality of frontier models at a fraction of the cost and runtime. On top of that, training the model yourself yields greater ownership and flexibility: the resulting checkpoint can be deployed in any location, further refined, or even used locally.
At Together, we want to empower every AI developer with the ability to get the best model for their task, as conveniently as possible. Post-training a great model requires many iterations on data curation, training algorithms, and evaluation protocols. On top of that, infrastructure for RL is getting ever more complex, with a fine line between “an efficiency optimization” and “a silent bug that holds back your runs”. Doing so for large models reliably and at scale presents its own set of challenges.
Frontier labs have entire teams solving each of the above problems. Since tackling all challenges at once is a big investment, many companies that could benefit from post-training never start it, or start and stall. Together Post-Training handles all optimizations and infrastructure without getting in the way, and our forward-deployed team partners with our customers to help with the end-to-end workflow. This lets every researcher or domain expert focus on what they do best while we take care of the rest.
Together Post-Training at a glance
As the complexity of post-training continues to evolve, so should the tooling around it. Together Post-Training provides a set of common abstractions familiar to ML developers, as well as control over the resources used by each experiment, while making sure that all computations under the hood are fast, cost-efficient, and, most importantly, correct.
We built our service to offer the highest degree of flexibility for your experiments. You can run LoRA training, including multiple LoRA adapters sharing the same GPU capacity, as well as full-weight experiments for select models. In contrast to our [fine-tuning service](https://www.together.ai/fine-tuning), the entire training loop of Together Post-Training is yours to define. You can use any data, environments, or agentic harnesses that suit your setup best, and add any steps you need (such as logging or external benchmarking) throughout the training process. The entire workflow is as follows:
All experiments run on Model Resources — GPU allocations that are fully yours, not competing with others’ requests for priority. Each Model Resource can hold one or several Training Sessions, where each one corresponds to a single experiment using the same base model (for example, one set of LoRA adapters). This means you get the best rollout and training performance, as you never have to compete with other users’ requests executing on the same hardware. At the same time, dedicated GPU allocations mean you can run full-weight finetuning, going beyond LoRA when adapting to large knowledge-intensive tasks.
Once you allocate the model resource and start the session, you can execute each step of the training loop. Each session contains a Trainer instance responsible for running forward/backward steps and updating the weights, as well as Generator instances for executing rollouts from the policy. For every model, we heavily optimize training and rollout performance, making sure all operations are fast and numerically aligned across stacks. In the case of SFT, you can start a model resource with 0 generators to save costs. You decide the point at which the trainer parameters are sent to the generator; we also support asynchronous RL for high GPU utilization of both components at all times, especially with long agentic rollouts.
While we support a number of standard losses (from cross-entropy and GRPO to CISPO and DPPO), we also allow computing a custom training objective locally and sending its gradients to the Trainer for computing the updates.
Together Post-Training launches with a range of leading open-weight models, including Muse Spark Open, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8-27B. We will expand the selection in the coming weeks, making sure you can use both the highest-capability frontier LLMs and efficient smaller models.
Quality, performance, and efficiency
Delegating the internals of post-training infrastructure can be a daunting decision. Our team has first-hand experience catching silent bugs in complex machine learning systems, from pushing the frontier of RL research to training LLMs that have served millions of users. We understand that the best training stack is the one that gets you the best model, and building such infrastructure demands careful implementation and co-design across all components.
For these reasons, we prioritized quality of output models as our north star in the development of the service. One notorious example of issues affecting RL results is the alignment between training and inference engines: if the same model weights produce slightly different outputs due to mismatching numerics, the whole run might underperform or even collapse. We eliminate numerous sources of policy drift across training and inference, using both standard techniques like [Rollout Routing Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370) and advanced optimizations driven by our research in training stability.
Beyond model quality, we also work to make each run as fast and as efficient as possible, because post-training requires multiple iterations: the sooner a run finishes and the less it costs, the more ideas you get to test. Most of the time in RL is spent on generating rollouts, which allows us to capitalize on years of research and engineering behind Together’s inference products. Our rollout engines draw on the same optimizations as our serving stack. For multi-turn agents, intelligent caching and routing minimize redundant computations while keeping memory costs bounded. On the training side, optimized parallelism and sequence packing speed up both SFT and RL steps.
With Together Post-Training, you size each experiment to what it needs and do not pay more. If your experiment is bottlenecked by rollout concurrency, you can request the exact number of sampler replicas. Several LoRA experiments can share one model resource, so running a sweep doesn’t mean reserving more GPUs for every setup. We bill every model resource per GPU-minute, yet thanks to many optimizations of our dedicated and multi-LoRA serving stacks, the overall costs of training drop below token-based pricing as soon as you scale up the experiments.
Optimized deployment after training
When the post-training experiments are finished, it might be important to run each resulting model side by side to compare their outputs. We now support [multi-LoRA adapter serving](https://docs.together.ai/docs/post-training/multi-lora-deployment) in Dedicated Model Inference: instead of starting a separate production deployment for each run, you can swap the adapters at your convenience in a single GPU deployment, helping you lower the serving costs.
Lastly, converting the model to run at the highest throughput in production means it potentially executes in lower precision, in a different hardware configuration, and with different kernels compared to rollout generation. Through a combination of algorithmic and systems improvements, we ensure that each training checkpoint retains the quality in serving, even after switching from multi-LoRA sampling to a fully performant [merged inference in FP4 precision](https://docs.together.ai/docs/post-training/prepare-for-fp4-inference).
Getting started
To begin your first post-training experiments, install the latest [Together SDK](https://github.com/togethercomputer/together-py) and [read the docs](https://docs.together.ai/docs/post-training/overview). We also provide a selection of cookbooks that can help you get started with Together Post-Training, which are available at [github.com/togethercomputer/post-training-cookbook](https://github.com/togethercomputer/post-training-cookbook). These cookbooks provide examples of training with GRPO on a standard GSM8K benchmark, implementing DPO as a custom loss, or training multiple LoRA adapters within the same model resource. If you already have a setup that uses post-training services such as Tinker API, we also offer a simple way to migrate from them. You can replace one line in your scripts, and everything else can stay the same:
Read our [Tinker migration guide](https://docs.together.ai/docs/post-training/migrate-from-tinker) to learn more.
How AI-native companies are using Together Post-Training today
Before this launch, we worked with a select group of organizations pushing the frontier of custom models. We granted them early access to our service over the past few months; the feedback we received was invaluable in developing the product which now everyone can use. Hear from the teams themselves:
“We had a great experience with the Together Post-Training platform from day one. The high degree of control and flexibility let us start running real RL experiments within a couple of hours. The service is efficient, allowing us to run up to five concurrent RL experiments on the same GPU capacity. The Together Research team was an exceptional collaborator throughout the training process, giving us feedback on model selection, training techniques, reward functions, and training efficiency.”
– Anthony Li, Associate Director of Data Science, [Deel](https://www.deel.com/)
“At Jack & Jill, we build two AI agents: Jack for professionals, and Jill for companies, who recruit from Jack’s network of professionals who’ve opted in to being introduced. We used Together Post-Training to post-train a model that predicts which candidates a hiring manager will want to meet, a core step in Jill’s search. Onboarding was easy, their team helped design our experiments, and their forward-deployed engineers wrote the scripts that got us to first results. We matched a closed-source model’s quality in offline evaluations, using an open-source model that’s significantly cheaper to serve.”
– Oliver Normand, Founding Engineer, [Jack & Jill](https://www.jackandjill.ai/)
“We’ve been collaborating with the Together team since the launch of its Post-Training beta in April. With the latest iteration, seamless self-onboarding made it easy to quickly launch full-scale agentic RL runs. The Post-Training service has proven to be exceptionally intuitive, flexible, and powerful for scaling sophisticated agentic workloads.”
– Adit Jain, Researcher, [Collinear AI](https://collinear.ai/)
Build with Together Post-Training
With the launch of Together Post-Training, we’re turning frontier-grade model customization into a reliable, flexible and efficient service. The next step is for you to make the most of it. For the first eight weeks, we are offering Together Post-Training at a reduced price of $9 per GPU-hour of B200 usage. Learn how to [get started](https://docs.together.ai/docs/post-training/quickstart-rl) today — we’re excited to see what you will build.
But you don’t have to do this alone. For companies that want a partner, our forward-deployed engineers work alongside your team acro

title: Investing in the public benefit
body:
Investing in the public benefit
Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed [$200 million](https://www.anthropic.com/news/economic-futures-research-fund-agenda) to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"
Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

## The challenge is to make the technology disappear

Creating a close, personalized experience for millions of customers in a country like Brazil is, first and foremost, a question of simplicity rather than of models.

“Much of it is about making something simple, direct, and useful, delivering a direct benefit to the customer, and making the technology almost unnoticeable,” says Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO of Itaú.

The standard he describes is demanding: the solution must solve a real everyday problem and be direct, simple, and memorable. Technology serves as the means, never as the centerpiece of the experience.

There is demand for this. A study by Itaú in partnership with Grupo Consumoteca shows that 80% of Brazilians want to better organize their financial lives and seek more effective support for decisions, and that 65% would like technologies that act as a financial copilot, providing ongoing guidance.

> “OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## ia.i: from convenience to advice, in one place

The journey began in 2024, when the bank introduced the first Inteligência Itaú capabilities for specific financial needs. ia.i is the next stage: a complete conversational layer, activated by text or voice, bringing interactions related to checking accounts, credit, cards, insurance, and other services into one environment — and connecting customers to specialized human support whenever needed.

This breadth was precisely what guided the choice of models.

“OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions,” Mazzei explains. “From the simplest ones, which need to be efficient in cost and latency, to more complex solutions, where reasoning and all the necessary grounding are required to provide an appropriate answer.”

Having a range of models — rather than a single model — made it possible to deliver the complete solution in one product. At the center of this experience is Customer DNA, a layer of financial context that helps the bank understand the needs, habits, and life stages of approximately 70 million customers. Under governance and responsible AI controls, GPT models are among the components that help maintain and enrich this representation, making interactions progressively more relevant.

The solution rests on three principles: interactivity, multimodality — text, voice, image, and clicks in the same experience — and individualization.

With approximately 300,000 customers in the first phase, the bank entered a period of learning about the real relationship between customer and product.

“We can understand how customers begin to use this product more deeply and see how it can directly benefit each person’s daily financial life,” says Mazzei. Its presence extends across the journey: from a question about an expense in an account statement to investment advice and convenient transactions on WhatsApp.

> “The financial world often has products that are not so straightforward and need this context, this simpler relationship with money.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## IARA: the layer that makes scale possible

Behind the visible experiences is an architectural decision. To operate AI at the scale of a bank, Itaú built IARA — a governance and orchestration platform that gives teams controlled access to different models in line with internal policies. OpenAI is among the model providers available in this environment.

This layer supports solutions such as the legal department’s, where the platform automates document reading, analysis, and interpretation. The solution operates on a repository of more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80% in stages of the department’s processes.

“It is essential that this information be preserved, remain within the bank’s context, and access models in a secure, governed way, with an understanding of token-use efficiency so that the entire solution is economically viable for the bank,” Mazzei says.

IARA addresses three problems at once: cost control per token, accuracy of responses, and application of responsible AI policies. In such a regulated sector, this makes it possible to move quickly while maintaining control.

“When we talk about Responsible AI at the bank, it is a discipline we take great care with,” he says. “We need customers to interact with the bank and our responses to align with our values and culture.” This includes reducing any risk of bias that may arise in frontier models.

Responsible AI principles guide the entire lifecycle of solutions, from development to continuous monitoring, aiming to ensure safety, transparency, ethics, and regulatory compliance as the technology scales.

> “IARA is a fundamental platform, because it ensures we can have governance and observability in a highly regulated environment.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## AI First on the inside, too

The bank’s AI First strategy extends beyond end customers. The same intelligence layer that supports ia.i also assists specialists, managers, and customer service teams.

Mazzei describes a range extending from automating simple tasks to performing work that was previously unfeasible — but adds value to customer relationships: summaries before meetings, meeting preparation, understanding a specific issue, and developing plans and alternatives that were previously less obvious and time-consuming.

The bank has significant expectations for this implementation: three times more time available for customer relationships, service up to twice as fast, and conversations up to three times more effective.

> “This set of tools in the hands of relationship managers allows us to focus on what matters most: creating value for our customers.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## Results overview

- ia.i reached approximately 300,000 customers in its first phase, covering everything from convenient transactions to investment advice, activated by text or voice.
- The IARA platform makes different models available to the bank’s teams with governance, observability, cost control per token, and enforcement of Responsible AI.
- The legal solution operates on more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80%.
- Using a range of models made it possible to serve both cost- and latency-sensitive cases and those requiring deeper reasoning; GPT‑5.x models are part of Customer DNA, which provides financial context for approximately 70 million customers.

## Lessons for leaders

- Measure the experience by its simplicity, rather than sophistication. The goal is for the technology to go unnoticed and the benefit to be apparent.
- Choose a range of models, rather than a single one. Real journeys combine low-latency interactions with decisions that require reasoning.
- Build the governance layer before scaling. Observability, cost control, and responsible AI make scale viable in regulated sectors.
- Treat bias and cultural alignment as product requirements. Responses to customers must reflect the institution’s values.
- Apply the strategy internally, too. Giving time back to teams frees up human relationships where they matter most.

## Tips

- Start with concrete everyday problems, such as a question about an account statement or a simple transaction.
- Launch to an initial customer group and use it to learn actual behavior before expanding.
- Centralize model access on one platform to maintain control over costs and quality.
- Monitor token efficiency from day one — economic viability is part of the design.
- Combine conversation and navigation: not every action is best handled through natural language.

## Next steps

ia.i continues to evolve. The bank expects to make the experience available to its entire customer base by the end of 2026. Planned capabilities for the next stages include product simulations and sign-ups, as well as recurring financial analyses of income, expenses, and habits.

For Mazzei, the significance of the initiative goes beyond the product — the bank has navigated decades of transformation, with customers’ habits and expectations constantly changing.

> “Leading the AI era is about responding faster to our customers’ needs. It is about understanding how technology can add value and help customers engage with financial products and services in a much simpler, more direct way that helps them achieve what they are seeking.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú
