title: An update on independent evaluators
body:
An update on independent evaluators
Last month, we committed to [stronger independent, third-party assessment](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from [METR](https://metr.org/), a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.
METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on [several reviews of our Risk Reports](https://metr.org/risk-assessment/). We’re also working with [SecureBio](https://securebio.org/) and [Accenture](https://www.anthropic.com/news/accenture-embedded-evaluation) as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/).
Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.
Why we work with independent evaluators
As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.
To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:
- Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as
[alignment faking](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking). - Independence: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
- Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
- Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process.
Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.
For the AI industry, this is a step toward [robust safety oversight](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/0a58d567024a8b448ff15158ebc3625328dfcc1f.pdf). We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.
What we mean by “employee-like access”
We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.[1](#footnote-1)
METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, predefined categories like the ones above. METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information.
Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.
Our other evaluator partnerships
We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.
We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.
In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.
In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.
The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.
SecureBio is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our [August Risk Report](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/f61d49fa5596956a5dec75fea0e973bf6a6a8378/Redacted%20Risk%20Report%20August%202026%20.pdf), after completing and [publishing a pilot review](https://securebio.org/resources/anthropic_feb_2026_risk_review.pdf) of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.[2](#footnote-2)
With Accenture and Faculty, we're working [toward an ambitious partnership](https://www.anthropic.com/news/accenture-embedded-evaluation) that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.
We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.

Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.

title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
body:
Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
[MLX](https://mlx-framework.org/) on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. [In a previous post](/research/exploring-llms-mlx-m5), we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.
In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model â Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters â right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see [Figure 1](#figure1)), well above average human reading speed.
Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.
[Running Large Language Models with MLX](#running-large-language-models-with-mlx)
We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on [Mac Studio](https://www.apple.com/mac-studio/specs/), using the MLX LM package, as described in our [prior post](/research/exploring-llms-mlx-m5#running--llms-on-apple-silicon). We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.
We evaluate three frontier-class models ([Table 1](#table1)) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts â and thus parameters â active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).
| Model | Total Parameters | Active Parameters | Native Precision | Evaluation Precision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | 816B | 42B | BF16 | NVFP4 |
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 128B | 128B | FP8 | FP8 |
| Qwen 3.8 | 27B | 27B | BF16 | BF16 |
Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark
. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:
mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1
A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.
Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in [Table 2](#table2) and [Table 3](#table3), respectively.
[Inference Performance on a Single Mac Studio](#inference-performance-on-a-single-mac-studio)
Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In [Figure 2](#figure2), we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.
Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6Ã faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see [Figure 2](#figure2)). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.
Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see [Figure 3](#figure3)), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6Ã faster tokens/s.
The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see [Figure 4](#figure4)): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra â a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.
While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.
[Pipelining Inference Across Two Mac Studio Computers](#pipelining-inference-across-two-mac-studio-computers)
Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the modelâs inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the modelâs layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see [Figure 5](#figure5)) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.
MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the [MLX distributed documentation](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/usage/distributed.html). These rely on fast inter-machine communication: [macOS 26.2](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-26_2-release-notes) introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (jaccl
, pronounced âjackalâ) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl
uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch
, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline
In this command, --backend jaccl
specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1
flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).
In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see [Figure 7](#figure7)) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.
It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill â up to ~1.8Ã faster (see [Figure 6](#figure6)). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192
) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk , the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk , so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.
[Tensor Parallelization for Faster Inference](#tensor-parallelization-for-faster-inference)
Tensor parallelization (see [Figure 5](#figure5)) distributes the LLMâs width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl
, is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.
With MLXâs high-level mlx.launch
helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1
[Figure 8](#figure8) and [Figure 9](#figure9) show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.
With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the expertsâ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.
The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s â the two-cable value reported in [Table 2](#table2), the one-cable run being an additional experiment.
Time to First Token (seconds)
Lower is better
| Model | M3 Ultra | M5 Ultra | 2 M5 Pipeline | 2 M5 Tensor | 4 M5 Tensor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | â | â | 8.4 | 8.2 | 4.8 |
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 95.9 | 24.6 | 24.5 | 14.4 | 7.5 |
| Qwen 3.8 | 18.2 | 4.1 | 4.1 | 3.1 | 1.7 |
Decode Speed (tokens per second)
Higher is better
| Model | M3 Ultra | M5 Ultra | 2 M5 Pipeline | 2 M5 Tensor | 4 M5 Tensor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | â | â | 15.74 | 24.99 | 36.73 |
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 4.95 | 7.70 | 7.70 | 13.69 | 23.37 |
| Qwen 3.8 | 12.46 | 19.69 | 19.44 | 33.27 | 50.89 |

title: Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
body:
[content type paper](/research/)published October 2026
Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
AuthorsMingfei Zhang, Amit Surana, Ziauddin Majid, Chenxi Wang, Michael Xu
Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
AuthorsMingfei Zhang, Amit Surana, Ziauddin Majid, Chenxi Wang, Michael Xu
Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry. Evaluating on ToolBench (46,984 unique API endpoints, 50 categories) across single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2), and cross-category multi-tool (G3) query subsets, we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single-tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries. This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (k=1 to 20), is robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and is consistent across model families (Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt-oss-120b). We characterize a stub-hallucination failure mode (the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names) that acts as a double-edged sword: on simple queries PtRâs stubs abstract away proper-noun signals that RtP matches directly, yet on complex queries the same mechanism decomposes multi-faceted intent into functional sub-needs. We further analyze token overhead and show that PtRâs extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost, which pays off on multi-tool queries but hurts on single-tool ones, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical directionâone that can be driven by a zero-cost signal already present in the pipeline (RtPâs top-1 retrieval score).
ProTIP: Progressive Tool Retrieval Improves Planning

title: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents
body:
Multimodal agents commonly generate freeform reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from the reasoning candidates based on their likelihoods given the current context, without an auxiliary task head. Using pre-specified reasoning traces enables parallel scoring, where teacher-forced prefilling computes token likelihoods concurrently within and across candidates using a shared context KV cache. We evaluated SSR on seven multimodal search benchmarks using 2B and 4B models. Across multiple reinforcement learning objectives and supervised fine-tuning, SSR delivers significant efficiency gains without sacrificing task performance. SSR achieves an average success rate competitive with leading search agents of the same scale, while reducing per-turn reasoning latency by over 90% and total per-question model inference latency by 28â54%.

title: Code Review is now generally available
body:
Code Review is now generally available
Catch more bugs before they reach production.
Code Review is out of research preview and available to Claude Team and Enterprise organizations.
Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Code Review credits by January 15, 2027. Credits expire 30 days after you claim them.[Terms apply.]
What's new in Code Review
Coding agents keep increasing the pace at which teams write code, and the review bottleneck hasn't eased. For general availability, we made Code Review faster, better at finding the bugs that matter, and easier to tune to each of your repositories.
Since we released the [research preview](https://claude.com/resources/articles/code-review), Code Review has gotten sharper, catching more of the bugs that would otherwise reach production. We also run Code Review on pull requests at Anthropic, which shows us where reviews slow our own engineers down. Teams using Code Review during the preview told us the rest: it was catching real issues before a human reviewer looked at the PR, but they wanted reviews that were quieter, sized to each change, and faster. Here’s what we shipped:
- Speed: Most reviews now finish about 3x faster (~20 minutes down to 6-10 minutes) compared to during preview.
- Quality: Find more of the bugs that matter, with clear, concise findings that state the problem, what triggers it, and the fix in a few sentences.
- Flexibility: Admins choose Quick, Standard (default), or Deep for each repository, so routine codebases get a quick pass and the most critical ones get a deep review. Every level delivers high-quality reviews.
Get started
Code Review is now generally available for Team and Enterprise plans.
- For admins: Enable Code Review in your
[Claude Code settings](http://claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code), install the GitHub App, and select repositories you’d like to run reviews on. - For developers: Once enabled, reviews run automatically on new PRs. No configuration needed.

title: Agent sprawl: How to manage agent proliferation in the enterprise
body:
The growth of [enterprise AI agent platforms](https://cohere.com/blog/introducing-north-2) has made it much easier for employees to build and deploy agents to support their own work.
But as agent creation becomes more decentralized, enterprises face a new management problem: how to keep track of what agents have been built across the organization. Without that visibility, teams can struggle to find and reuse existing agents, while access to enterprise data and systems can become harder to govern. When this proliferation of agents becomes too difficult to manage, it becomes agent sprawl.
In this article, we’ll explain why proliferation isn’t inherently bad, explore how enterprises tend to manage agent sprawl, and consider an alternative approach that allows variant agents to compete.
Build reusable agents and automations and share them across the enterprise with North 2: our secure, agentic AI platform that runs where your data lives.
Why agent proliferation isn’t necessarily a bad thing
The same tools that create the potential for agent sprawl also make experimentation much easier. Employees no longer need to rely exclusively on a central AI or engineering team every time they identify a task that could benefit from an agent. Instead, they can [build and test agents](https://cohere.com/blog/building-ai-agents) themselves, tailored to the specifics of the work they’re trying to augment.
This kind of decentralized experimentation is valuable. First, those closest to a workflow are often best placed to determine how it could be streamlined by an agent. Second, when useful agents can be shared and reused, a solution initially developed for one team can be adopted by other teams facing a similar problem. So at an organizational level, proliferation can be a sign that employees are actively testing new ideas and discovering useful applications for agents.
This raises the question of whether having a growing number of agents always creates more overhead. After all, more agents don’t necessarily mean higher inference costs — an agent that isn’t being used doesn’t consume tokens simply because it exists. Instead, the management burden appears when the process for managing agents fails to keep pace with their growing numbers. That’s when agent proliferation is better described as agent sprawl.
Proliferation can be a sign that employees are actively testing new ideas and discovering useful applications for agents.
How enterprises currently manage agent sprawl
Enterprises today typically manage growing agent estates with one of the following approaches:
- Centralized delivery: A central AI or engineering team builds and governs agents for the rest of the organization. This can offer tighter control, but can limit the pace of innovation.
- Federated delivery: Business units or individual teams own agent development and operation, while central functions provide shared infrastructure, standards, and
[governance patterns](https://cohere.com/blog/ai-governance-challenges). - Hybrid delivery: Central and business teams share responsibility for building and operating agents under common standards and governance patterns.
Across these operating models, enterprises are increasingly using agent registries to maintain a shared view of their agent estates. A registry helps an organization keep track of agent ownership, usage, and access permissions, while helping employees discover agents that already exist. This setup reinforces a common preference for avoiding duplication. Teams should default to reusing existing solutions before building something new.
Of course, there are good reasons to limit unnecessary duplication. It’s an obvious way to reduce sprawl: employees have fewer overlapping options to sift through, while the enterprise has fewer agents to monitor and govern.
But treating duplication as something to avoid in every case can also suppress innovation. If the mere existence of a workable agent means no alternatives should be built, organizations forfeit the opportunity to discover solutions that are cheaper, more reliable, or better suited to the task.
Treating duplication as something to avoid in every case can suppress innovation.
An alternative approach: Allow agent variants to compete
How can enterprises make room for useful duplication without letting it develop into agent sprawl?
One way is to treat duplication as provisional rather than permanent. If a team has a credible reason to believe it can improve on an “incumbent” agent, it should be permitted to build a “challenger” variant. However, the continued use of the challenger should depend on whether it demonstrates a meaningful advantage over the incumbent.
This competitive model requires a time-bounded, evidence-based comparison between the incumbent and challenger. Specific metrics will depend on the use case, but could include measures such as reliability, token use, and latency, as well as task performance.
Once enough evidence has been collected to make a meaningful comparison, the organization can decide whether the challenger should replace the incumbent or be retired. If the challenger proves better suited to a part of the incumbent’s workload, both agents might remain as distinct alternatives.
For example, consider a bank’s commercial lending division, where a central team has built a [finance agent](https://cohere.com/blog/ai-agents-for-financial-services) that drafts credit memos for relationship managers. A lending team that handles routine annual reviews believes it can do better, so it builds a challenger designed for the same range of tasks using a smaller, cheaper model and an additional step that cross-checks financial figures against supporting documents.
For 30 days, both agents draft memos for a representative set of cases, from routine annual reviews to more complex financing cases. The bank compares them on four measures: how many figures trace correctly to their source documents, how heavily credit officers edit each draft, token cost per memo, and time to first draft.
If the challenger delivers comparable quality across the different types of work at a substantially lower cost, it replaces the incumbent. If it falls short without offering any meaningful advantage, it’s retired. And if it wins on routine annual reviews but struggles with complex new financings, both agents stay — each assigned to the work it handles best.
It’s therefore necessary to tolerate some duplication for this approach to work, but only insofar as that duplication creates useful competition. Once testing reveals that one competing agent offers no advantage over the other, there’s no reason for both to remain.
Final thoughts
Avoiding agent sprawl does not require eliminating duplication altogether.
Some duplication — or variation — is necessary if enterprises want to compare competing approaches.
The key is to pair variation with selection pressure. By making agent creation easy but persistence conditional, enterprises can preserve the benefits of continuous experimentation without sliding into sprawl.

title: AI for utilities requires capability and control
body:
[Energy and utility companies](https://cohere.com/solutions/energy-and-utilities) are increasingly using AI to transform many aspects of their operations. Common use cases include strengthening cyber and infrastructure defenses, making engineering knowledge easier to find, and reducing the time that employees spend assembling information. Realizing this value requires the same discipline that utilities apply to other consequential technologies, including processes to define operating boundaries, validate performance, and ensure accountability.
For an organization responsible for critical energy infrastructure, model capability is only one part of the purchasing decision. Where AI runs, what information it can access, and what authority it receives determine which workloads a utility can responsibly put into production.
Recent discussions between frontier AI labs and utility executives illustrate an important tension facing critical-infrastructure operators.
The question for utilities is no longer simply: “What can this model do?”
It is also: Where does it run? What information can it access? What actions can it take? How is it monitored? And who remains in control?
[Cohere North](https://cohere.com/north) is designed to address these questions and much more.
In this post, we’ll take a look at key considerations for utility leaders and how North can meet a utility organization’s security, data, and operational requirements.
Recent AI developments raise the stakes
OpenAI’s recent engagement with utilities reflects the growing role of AI in critical-infrastructure cybersecurity. Its September [Daybreak announcement](https://openai.com/index/daybreak-for-frontline-defenders/) describes a gathering of utility leaders whose organizations cover 40 states and Washington, D.C. and collectively serve more than half the US population. The initiative aims to help utilities identify vulnerabilities, analyze suspicious activity, and develop and test fixes.
The opportunity comes with a clear reminder about control. In OpenAI’s [August incident report](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/), the company described how models undergoing internal cybersecurity evaluations in July circumvented isolation controls, communicated through unauthorized channels, and compromised parts of its research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems. The evaluations used reduced safeguards, and the disclosure does not establish that utility grid-control systems were compromised. OpenAI described subsequent measures to strengthen isolation, monitoring, and alignment.
For utility leaders, these developments underscore a practical point: greater AI capability must be accompanied by secure deployment boundaries.
Five questions every AI proposal should answer
- What measurable problem will this solve? Define the workflow, establish a baseline, and evaluate output quality alongside speed.
- What can the agent actually do? Specify which systems the agent can access, what actions it can take, and which human approvals are required.
- What information leaves our environment? Identify every external dependency. Follow the data through the entire workflow, including document processing, model inference, storage, logs, integrations, telemetry, and support access.
- How will recommendations be validated? Require traceability of supporting source material and associated citations, along with human-in-the-loop evaluations by subject matter experts (SMEs).
- What happens after the pilot? Establish a licensing agreement that provides commercial predictability throughout the path to full production and mitigates token shock.
A different approach: Bring AI to the utility’s data
Cohere’s approach to [enterprise AI](https://cohere.com/blog/enterprise-ai) is to deliver the models to the data that utilities need to protect. Rather than requiring organizations to redesign sensitive workflows around a public AI service, Cohere’s North platform can be deployed within the operator’s secure perimeter, which can fundamentally expand where utilities are able to use AI.
North creates a path for utilities to work with engineering documents, asset histories, emergency procedures, customer information, and internal operating knowledge within their controlled environments without the potential for data egress. This allows operators to select an architecture that fits the sensitivity of the workload and its requirements [for control over data and infrastructure](https://cohere.com/blog/ai-infrastructure).
The following considerations can help utilities ensure a successful rollout of AI across their organization.
Keep authority and accountability with the utility
As [AI agents](https://cohere.com/blog/ai-agents) become more capable, one principle becomes essential: the organization deploying an AI agent must decide what it is authorized to do. With built-in access controls, audit visibility, and configurable workflows, North combines enterprise-grade performance with robust governance. This allows organizations to define what information individual workflows can access and what authority their integrations receive.
A sensible starting point would be to use North to create an agent that retrieves approved information, compares documents, identifies inconsistencies, and prepares recommendations for employee review. Its authority can expand after the agent demonstrates reliable performance and the organization verifies that its safeguards are effective. Note that access to production or operational systems should require separate authorization and appropriate approval controls, enforced through identity, network, and application permissions.
Good [governance frameworks, practices, and policies](https://cohere.com/blog/ai-governance) make those boundaries durable. Each workflow should have an accountable owner, approved uses, evaluation criteria, and a change-control process. Traceability should connect a recommendation to its source records and preserve the relevant versions, approvals, and execution logs. Teams also need a tested way to stop a workflow and investigate failures.
[Private deployment](https://cohere.com/private-deployments) supports a secure operating model that creates a deliberate path from AI that informs to AI that acts, with the utility controlling that progression.
Put institutional knowledge to work
Much of the near-term value from AI can come from helping employees use information that the utility already owns. For example, an engineer could use AI to assemble an asset’s maintenance history before it is reviewed. A storm response team could quickly locate the applicable section of an approved emergency plan. Or a regulatory team could gather supporting records for a filing.
[AI-powered enterprise search and retrieval ](https://cohere.com/blog/enterprise-search)can reduce the effort required to find that material. It gives employees the ability to inspect the search output’s supporting sources, check that guidance is current, and resolve conflicting records before relying on an answer. These workflows can also help newer employees learn from documented experience as long-serving colleagues retire while preserving the role of professional judgment.
Build a business case that lasts
A shared AI platform creates an opportunity to reuse approved infrastructure, integrations, and governance across departments. That said, each additional use case should still earn its place through measured results.
A strong business case for a particular project includes licensing, hardware requirements, integration, support, security operations, and ongoing evaluation. It includes a rollout plan that starts with a bounded workflow, then measures the results, and finally expands only when both the value and the controls are demonstrated. This gives the project a defensible basis for investment, and provides the organization with a repeatable method for deciding where AI belongs.
The goal should not be to deploy AI everywhere. It should be to create a controlled foundation on which additional use cases can be introduced when their value has been demonstrated.
Conclusion
By enabling utilities to deploy AI within environments they control, connect it securely to their own knowledge, define access and agent authority, and expand automation as performance and safeguards are demonstrated, North provides a practical foundation for enterprise AI in critical infrastructure.
The opportunity is to combine increasingly capable AI with something utilities have always required: operational discipline, clear accountability, and control over the systems on which their customers depend. For utilities, this operational discipline is part of the value proposition from the first deployment.
Interested in exploring what controlled, private AI could look like for your utility? [Contact Cohere](https://cohere.com/contact-sales) to learn more about North for utilities and how it can be deployed to meet your organization’s security, data, and operational requirements.

title: AI ROI: How enterprises can measure the return on AI investments
body:
Enterprises investing in AI need to know whether the expected business value justifies the cost, and whether that value is actually being realized once AI is deployed.
But measuring enterprise AI ROI presents some distinct challenges. AI costs can vary with how systems are designed, deployed, and used, while operational improvements in speed and productivity don’t always translate cleanly into financial value.
In this post, we’ll unpack what makes AI ROI difficult to calculate, and explain how enterprises can account for those difficulties when forecasting and measuring returns.
What is AI ROI?
AI ROI is the financial return generated by an AI investment relative to the total cost of deploying and operating it. That return can be realized through cost savings, additional profit from sales, or both.
ROI can be calculated as: ROI = (financial benefit - total cost) ÷ total cost x 100
Importantly, the operational improvements brought about by AI don’t necessarily translate directly into financial returns. Faster task completion, greater output, or higher-quality work may well produce financial value, but a positive ROI ultimately depends on whether that value exceeds the cost of achieving it with AI.
What makes AI ROI difficult for enterprises to forecast and measure?
The key challenge in calculating the ROI of AI is establishing the costs and returns that belong in the calculation.
AI costs accumulate across the [technical infrastructure](https://cohere.com/blog/ai-infrastructure) and operational resources required to deploy and run it. At the same time, returns from AI can be hard to isolate since the technology is typically embedded in wider business processes.
Here are some of the distinctive characteristics of AI investment that can make its ROI especially difficult to calculate.
AI unit economics can shift with workload and scale
In generative and [agentic AI](https://cohere.com/blog/what-is-agentic-ai) applications, the cost of completing a task can vary with the work involved. All else being equal, tasks that use longer context, require more reasoning, or involve more model and tool calls cost more to execute. Agentic systems can add further variability by executing similar tasks with different numbers of steps, retries, or tool calls.
Scaling AI use changes the economics in other ways. While higher usage generally increases total variable costs, it can improve the utilization of existing capacity before more capacity needs to be provisioned.
Pilot-stage unit costs may also differ from those at production scale, since production use can expose the system to larger and more varied workloads.
Model and deployment choices reshape the cost-performance tradeoff
Models vary considerably in cost, speed, and performance. Higher-cost models can be better suited to more demanding tasks, while less expensive models are often sufficient for simpler workloads. One emerging approach is cost-aware model routing: AI applications draw on multiple models and direct each task to the lowest-cost model that meets its performance requirements.
Deployment choices also change the cost structure of running AI. For enterprises with lower volume or less predictable demand, usage-based managed services can be economical because they pay only for what they use without committing to a fixed amount of capacity. By contrast, dedicated capacity — whether provider-hosted or self-managed — can offer better unit economics for high, sustained workloads. However, this approach can leave paid-for capacity underutilized if demand is low or uneven.
For most enterprises, cost is only one consideration: latency, data residency, security requirements, and operational control can all determine which deployment options are viable.
Further reading: [The total cost of AI ownership](https://cohere.com/blog/the-total-cost-of-ai-ownership)
Meeting AI quality and reliability requirements can increase operating costs
Inference costs don’t always capture the full cost of delivering outputs at the quality and reliability required for production use. Enterprises may need to monitor output consistency and system behavior over time, run automated validation checks, and route uncertain or high-risk cases for human review. These activities add compute, tooling, and labor costs.
The amount of additional overhead depends on the use case. High-stakes or error-sensitive workflows may require more extensive evaluation and oversight. For agentic systems, evaluation may also need to cover the sequence of tool calls and actions taken during execution, not just final outputs.
Task-level efficiency gains can overstate enterprise-level financial value
AI can make an individual task more efficient without necessarily improving the economics of the wider process. If another step remains constrained, the efficiency gain may simply shift the bottleneck elsewhere rather than increase overall throughput or reduce end-to-end completion time.
AI can make an individual task more efficient without improving the economics of the wider process.
A practical approach to forecasting and measuring enterprise AI ROI
Given the difficulty of establishing the costs and financial value of AI with confidence, the figures used in an ROI estimate need to be well grounded, and any assumptions used to derive them should be explicit and open to testing.
The following considerations can help enterprises build and test more credible estimates.
Translate AI-driven process improvements into financial value
Enterprises can use a pre-AI baseline to measure how process outcomes change after AI is introduced. However, a simple before-and-after comparison may be misleading if other conditions change at the same time. For example, sales might rise after an AI tool is introduced simply because demand happened to increase at the same time. A/B tests, staggered rollouts, or comparisons between similar teams using and not using AI can help tease out how much of the change is due to AI rather than those other effects.
Once an improvement can be attributed to AI, enterprises can quantify its financial value. This can be relatively straightforward when the financial effect of the improvement can be measured directly — like if AI increases conversion rates and the additional sales generate $200,000 in gross profit.
Other improvements are harder to value because their financial effects are further downstream. For example, an [AI-enabled manufacturing process](https://cohere.com/blog/ai-in-manufacturing-and-supply-chain) might lower the defect rate, which in turn lowers rework, returns, or warranty costs. In cases like this, enterprises need to estimate the financial value of the AI-driven improvement from the resulting cost savings.
Establish the full cost of delivering AI in production
Model and inference costs are among the most visible costs of running AI, but they represent only part of the total cost. A credible ROI estimate also includes upfront implementation costs and ongoing technical and operational costs, such as infrastructure, integrations, monitoring, human oversight, and engineering support.
Model and inference costs are among the most visible costs of running AI, but they represent only part of the total cost.
Some of those costs are easy to miss because they sit inside existing technology or operating budgets rather than appearing as separate AI expenses. For example, if engineers spend part of their time maintaining AI-related integrations, or if AI workloads consume centrally funded infrastructure capacity, the ROI calculation should reflect the cost of the resources AI actually uses.
Stress-test ROI at production scale and over an appropriate time horizon
Enterprises can sharpen their ROI forecasts by testing them against several plausible production scenarios. For example, they can vary assumptions about expected usage volume, workload mix, production costs, and financial value to see which factors matter most and how far they can change before the business case breaks down. Once AI is in production, enterprises can use actual usage, cost, and financial data to update those forecasts.
The forecast’s time horizon matters too. AI investments can incur significant upfront costs before their full benefits are realized, so a short forecast period can understate AI’s longer-term returns. But longer-range forecasts also become less reliable given the unpredictability of future changes to AI costs, capabilities, and business conditions. Enterprises can manage that tradeoff by modeling ROI over several future time horizons to see when the investment is expected to break even and how much of the projected return depends on longer-term assumptions.
Final thoughts
ROI analysis helps enterprises decide where to scale, redesign, or pull back AI use as model capabilities improve and costs change. As teams gain experience with AI, they may also develop entirely new AI-enabled products, services, or ways of working that weren’t part of the original business case. Enterprises can then assess the value created by these innovations relative to what the business would likely have achieved without them.

title: Cohere and AISLE sign letter of intent to advance cyber-resilient sovereign AI
body:
Today Cohere announced a proposed agreement to acquire AISLE, the company building autonomous systems to discover and remediate previously unknown vulnerabilities in critical software.
The proposed transaction represents another important step in Cohere's mission to build the world's leading sovereign AI platform, combining frontier AI models, agentic applications, secure deployment infrastructure, and advanced security capabilities that enable organizations to deploy AI with confidence.
It also reflects our continued investment in Europe. Following our acquisitions of Reliant AI and Aleph Alpha, the addition of AISLE would deepen our presence across the region and strengthen European AI and cybersecurity capabilities that help protect critical infrastructure, governments, and highly regulated industries around the world.
Security is becoming the defining challenge of enterprise AI
As organizations move AI from experimentation to production, security has become one of the most important factors determining successful adoption.
Enterprises and governments are increasingly navigating complex requirements around data protection, governance, regulatory compliance, software vulnerabilities, and the risks associated with more autonomous AI systems. At the same time, they are looking for AI partners that can deliver the flexibility to operate in private cloud, on-premises, and fully air-gapped environments without compromising security or control.
Addressing these security challenges requires more than powerful models. It requires a full-stack approach that brings together AI, cybersecurity, governance, and secure deployment. That's why we're excited about the opportunity to bring AISLE's expertise into Cohere.
Why AISLE
Founded in 2024, AISLE has developed innovative AI systems capable of discovering, validating and helping remediate previously unknown vulnerabilities in complex production software. Its approach combines increasingly capable foundation models with specialized security expertise, large-scale code analysis, rigorous validation and automated remediation.
In its first year out of stealth, AISLE discovered more than [500 previously unknown vulnerabilities assigned CVEs](https://aisle.com/blog/aisle-year-on-the-cyber-frontier) across more than 100 codebases, including all 12 vulnerabilities in OpenSSL's January security release and [18 of the 24 CVEs in curl's latest release](https://aisle.com/blog/one-aisle-curl-audit-produced-24-cves-18-ship-today). These real-world zero-day vulnerabilities are independently reviewed by the relevant software maintainers, demonstrating the growing capabilities of autonomous AI security systems.
AISLE's results also highlight an important insight: the capabilities of a foundation model and the specialized system built around it can reinforce each other. By bringing AISLE's autonomous security research closer to Cohere's frontier-model development and training, we see an opportunity to build more capable cybersecurity systems while exploring how difficult, verifiable security problems can help evaluate and improve future models.
Founders take Cohere leadership roles within newly-formed Cohere Cyber, with Prague set for expansion
AISLE’s team is joining Cohere, with its three founders taking leadership roles spanning cybersecurity, corporate security, AI security research and frontier model development.
Ondrej Vlcek will become Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber, and will lead the newly-established global cybersecurity business. Jaya Baloo will become Cohere’s Chief Information Security Officer, leading security across the company. Stanislav Fort will become Vice President, AI Security, joining Cohere’s core model research and training efforts and leading its AI security research.
Cohere also plans to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague, expanding AISLE’s existing presence and establishing the city as its global center for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems.
Strengthening Europe's role in the future of AI
Europe is becoming increasingly important in the development of sovereign AI. Governments and enterprises across the region are seeking technology partners that can deliver advanced AI capabilities while meeting stringent requirements around security, privacy, compliance, and data sovereignty. Cohere has made significant investments to support those needs, and this deal would further expand our ability to serve customers across Europe and globally.
What this means for customers
AISLE's technology will strengthen Cohere's ability to help customers build and operate secure, cyber-resilient AI systems.
The combined capabilities are expected to enhance Cohere’s ability to:
- Deliver advanced security and threat detection capabilities across enterprise and public sector deployments.
- Strengthen governance, monitoring, and observability for AI agents and autonomous workflows.
- Improve protections for sensitive organizational data and mission-critical systems.
- Support secure AI deployments across private cloud, on-premises, and fully air-gapped environments.
- Advance the development of cyber-resilient AI systems capable of identifying, prioritizing, and responding to emerging threats.
Looking ahead
At Cohere, we've long believed that organizations should maintain control over their AI strategy, data, infrastructure and governance. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in critical workflows, securing the software these systems depend on is becoming just as important.
Increasingly capable AI systems are transforming both cybersecurity and the threats organizations face, and defensive capabilities must advance just as quickly. By combining AISLE's autonomous vulnerability research with Cohere's frontier models and sovereign AI platform, we aim to make discovering, validating and fixing software vulnerabilities a continuous, scalable capability that helps protect critical systems.
We're excited about what we can build together and look forward to officially welcoming the AISLE team to Cohere.

title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
body:
Image-to-Image • 6B • Updated • 3.24k • 312
[
](#welcome-flux3-image-klein-in-diffusers-the-latest-open-image-generation-model-from-black-forest-labs)
Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers: The latest open image generation model from Black Forest Labs
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/flux-3.md)
[Black Forest Labs](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs)FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.
Both open checkpoints are in the [FLUX.3 Image Klein collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein):
| Checkpoint | What it is | Defaults |
|---|---|---|
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein |
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base
You can head on to the [Hugging Face space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein) and generate some images right now!
[
](#tldr)
TL;DR
- One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control.
- The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100.
- NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with
from_single_file
, for smaller GPUs. - LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing.
- Ships as a
[Modular Diffusers](#modular-diffusers)pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own.
[
](#contents)
Contents
[Getting started](#getting-started)[What FLUX.3 can do](#what-flux3-can-do)[Base model and quantized variants](#base-model-and-quantized-variants)[LoRA finetuning](#lora-finetuning)[What it costs to run](#what-it-costs-to-run)[The architecture](#the-architecture)[Modular Diffusers](#modular-diffusers)[Try it](#try-it)
[
](#getting-started)
Getting started
Install the latest diffusers
and transformers
(for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):
pip install -U diffusers transformers
Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:
import torch
from diffusers import ModularPipeline
pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein")
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.to("cuda")
pipe(prompt="a red fox", output="images")[0].save("fox.png")
[
](#what-flux3-can-do)
What FLUX.3 can do
[
](#text-to-image)
Text-to-image
FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The [official prompting guide](https://docs.bfl.ai/guides/prompting_summary) from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024
image in 16
steps by default. Pass height
, width
, or num_inference_steps
to change them.
prompt = (
"A wide-angle wildlife photograph of a red fox standing alert in a snow-covered forest clearing at golden hour. "
"The fox is centered in the frame, its thick orange winter coat contrasting with the fresh white snow, breath "
"visible in the cold air. Snow-laden pine trees fill the softly blurred background, and low warm sunlight rakes "
"across the scene from the left, casting long blue shadows."
)
fox = pipe(
prompt=prompt,
generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
output="images"
)[0]
fox.save("fox.png")
[
](#image-to-image)
Image-to-image
Pass a reference image (or more) with the image
argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.
prompt = (
"The same red fox in the same snow-covered forest clearing, now at night under a full moon: cool blue "
"moonlight, deep shadows, stars visible through the pine branches, the fox's eyes catching the light."
)
night = pipe(
prompt=prompt,
image=fox, # from the previous text to image example
generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
output="images",
)[0]
night.save("night.png")
With several references, refer to them in the prompt as <ref_image_0>
, <ref_image_1>
, ... in the order they are passed to image
:
red_fox = pipe(prompt="a red fox", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
bench = pipe(prompt="a wooden bench", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
combined = pipe(
prompt="The fox from <ref_image_0> sitting on the wooden bench from <ref_image_1> in a snowy setting.",
image=[red_fox, bench],
output="images",
)[0]
combined.save("combined.png")
[
](#layout-control)
Layout control
Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id
, a bbox
, and a desc
, and the caption mentions it as <id>
.
Boxes are written as
[y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max]
, y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.
[
](#placing-regions-in-a-new-image)
Placing regions in a new image
layout_prompt = (
"Minimalist graphic illustration featuring a black silhouette of a person <silhouette_1> centered against a "
"solid, vibrant chartreuse background <background_1>. The figure is captured in a dynamic, mid-stride running "
"pose, facing toward the left side of the frame. "
'[{"id": "background_1", "bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "desc": "A flat field of neon yellow-green with a subtle '
'paper texture and fine, organic grain."}, {"id": "silhouette_1", "bbox": [150, 150, 850, 850], "desc": "A '
"black silhouette of a person in motion, made of dense stippled ink. The leading edges are solid; the trailing "
'arm and leg dissolve into coarse square pixels and scattered dots."}]'
)
runner = pipe(prompt=layout_prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
[
](#moving-regions-within-a-reference-image)
Moving regions within a reference image
For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox
in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox
in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.
This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:
from diffusers.utils import load_image
knight_image = load_image("knight_orig.png")
edit_prompt = (
"In <ref_image_0>, move the miniature grey amigurumi knight figure <knight_1> upwards and to the left along the "
"yarn cliff <cliff_1>. Keep the rest of the image completely unchanged, preserving the blurred yarn backdrop "
"<backdrop_1>, the large knitted dragon <dragon_1>, and the fiery orange thread <fire_1>. "
'[{"id": "knight_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [500, 150, 850, 350], "tgt_bbox": [194, 55, 544, 255], '
'"desc": "A miniature amigurumi knight crocheted from thick grey woolen yarn."}, '
'{"id": "backdrop_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], '
'"desc": "A soft, out-of-focus backdrop of cream and indigo knitted yarn."}, '
'{"id": "cliff_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], "tgt_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], '
'"desc": "A steep cliff of stacked yarn skeins in mustard, terracotta, and indigo."}, '
'{"id": "needle_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], "tgt_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], '
'"desc": "An oversized polished steel tapestry needle."}, '
'{"id": "dragon_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], '
'"desc": "A large, fluffy knitted dragon in terracotta and mustard yarn."}, '
'{"id": "fire_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], "tgt_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], '
'"desc": "Curled puffs of fiery orange angora thread suspended in mid-air."}]'
)
moved = pipe(prompt=edit_prompt, image=knight_image, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
[
](#base-model-and-quantized-variants)
Base model and quantized variants
[
](#base-model)
Base model
Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see [LoRA finetuning](#lora-finetuning)).
pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base")
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to("cuda")
pipe.guider = pipe.guider.new(guidance_scale=5.0) # optional
image = pipe(prompt=prompt, output="images")[0]
[
](#single-file-format-checkpoints)
Single-file format checkpoints
Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16
and in two quantized formats: fp8r
(rowwise FP8) and nvfp4
. Load any of them with from_single_file
, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.
from diffusers import BFLQuantizationConfig, Flux3Transformer2DModel, ModularPipeline
model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base"
variant = "fp8r" # or "nvfp4"
transformer = Flux3Transformer2DModel.from_single_file(
f"https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/variants/{variant}/model.safetensors",
config=model_id,
subfolder="transformer",
quantization_config=BFLQuantizationConfig(compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16),
dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id)
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.update_components(transformer=transformer)
pipe.to("cuda")
For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors
and drop quantization_config
.
| Variant | Fast kernels on | Other GPUs |
|---|---|---|
fp8r |
Compute capability 8.9+ (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell) | Weights are dequantized each step: lower memory, no speedup |
nvfp4 |
Blackwell, with flashinfer-python and flashinfer-cubin at the same version |
Same as above |
[
](#lora-finetuning)
LoRA finetuning
FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers
ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with [Ostris' AI Toolkit](https://github.com/ostris/ai-toolkit)).
Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the [ multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain](https://huggingface.co/datasets/multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain) dataset, triggered with
trtcrd
:accelerate launch train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein.py \
--pretrained_model_name_or_path="black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" \
--dataset_name="multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain" \
--caption_column="caption" \
--instance_prompt="trtcrd" \
--output_dir="trained-flux3-tarot-lora" \
--mixed_precision="bf16" \
--resolution=1024 \
--use_aspect_ratio_buckets \
--train_batch_size=1 \
--rank=16 \
--lora_alpha=16 \
--learning_rate=1e-4 \
--lr_scheduler="constant" \
--max_train_steps=1500 \
--validation_prompt="a trtcrd of a cat, tarot style" \
--validation_epochs=25 \
--seed=0 \
--push_to_hub
To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:
--gradient_checkpointing \ --cache_latents \ --use_8bit_adam
--gradient_checkpointing
recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower),--cache_latents
pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and--use_8bit_adam
keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.
A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at [ diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora](https://huggingface.co/diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora). More training features and configurations are documented in the
[DreamBooth FLUX.3 README](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/main/examples/dreambooth/README_flux3_klein.md).
For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py
) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as <ref_image_0>
.
See the [DreamBooth FLUX.3 README](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/main/examples/dreambooth/README_flux3_klein.md) for all options and the full image-to-image example.
